Product / Retention

Customer cohort retention rate

The percentage of paying customer accounts in a starting cohort that remain paying at the end of a defined period. Follow the original account IDs rather than allowing newly acquired customers to replenish the cohort.

Explore in the metric hierarchy ↗Open calculators →
Level 4Inspect the detail

The percentage of paying customer accounts in a starting cohort that remain paying at the end of a defined period. Follow the original account IDs rather than allowing newly acquired customers to replenish the cohort.

%

How we use it

We can build cohort tables to compare the durability of customers acquired through different channels, offers, or onboarding paths.

Transparent calculationStarting-cohort paying accounts remaining at period end ÷ paying accounts in the starting cohort × 100
starting cohort accounts200
remaining starting accounts190

190 ÷ 200 × 100 = 95% retention for the original customer cohort.

Illustrative calculation. Not a client result or a universal benchmark.

Break the result down

  • Starting account cohort
  • Plan and tenure
  • Market and customer segment

Questions we investigate

  • Are remaining accounts from the original cohort?
  • Which segments lose accounts over time?
  • Do new accounts accidentally inflate retention?

Actions the evidence supports

  • Track fixed cohort membership and status.
  • Investigate recurring cancellation causes.
  • Review adoption and revenue retention together.

Reporting contract

Ownership & cadence

Customer success analytics lead
Monthly and at agreed cohort milestones.

Required data

  • Starting paying account cohort
  • Period-end status of the same accounts
  • Account eligibility and merge rules

Read the measure with context

Zero starting accounts makes retention undefined. Account retention ignores changes in account revenue. Retention equals 100% minus churn only when both use identical cohort, period, and endpoint rules. Reactivation and merged-account treatment must be documented; product-usage retention is a separate measure.
